lessons.title: Lesson 1: The four kinds of AI tools a nonprofit uses
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Match a nonprofit task to the right kind of AI tool.
This lesson builds toward: Given a nonprofit task, you will choose the right kind of AI tool for it: chat assistant, office suite, design tool or meeting and note tool, getting at least 4 of 5 right.
Most nonprofit AI work fits four kinds of tools. Chat assistants (ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, Google Gemini) write, explain and summarize. Office suites (Microsoft 365, Google Workspace) have AI built into email, documents and spreadsheets.
Design tools (such as Canva or Adobe Express) help make flyers, social posts and slides, often with AI features. Meeting and note tools can record or transcribe a meeting and draft a summary, but only use them when everyone in the meeting agrees.
Start with one tool from each kind that your organization already has. Fewer tools, used well, beat many tools used once.
Words to know:
- Chat assistant: an AI you type or talk to that writes answers.
- Office suite: a set of work programs: email, documents, spreadsheets, slides.
- Transcribe: turn spoken words into written text.
Try it now: Write down the tools your organization already uses (email, documents, design). For each, note which of the four kinds it is.
You can now name the four kinds of AI tools and match a task to the right one.

check.q: Which kind of tool has AI built into email, documents and spreadsheets?
check.why: Office suites like Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace have AI built into everyday work programs.

check.q: Your team has tried eight AI tools once each. What does this lesson suggest?
options: Pick one tool from each kind that you already have and use it well
check.why: Fewer tools, used well, beat many tools used once.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Finding free and discounted nonprofit programs
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find out which nonprofit tech programs your organization may qualify for and where to apply.
This lesson builds toward: Using the official program pages, you will identify which nonprofit tech programs your organization may qualify for and what you need to apply, with current terms checked on the official page.
Big tech companies run nonprofit programs. Google for Nonprofits gives eligible registered charities no-cost or discounted Google products, including discounts on Google Workspace and Google Ad Grants, which gives qualifying nonprofits up to $10,000 a month in Google search ads. Google uses a partner called Goodstack to verify that you are a nonprofit.
Microsoft's nonprofit offers include Microsoft 365 Business Basic free for up to 300 users, discounted paid plans, and Copilot Chat included with a Microsoft 365 subscription. You register and Microsoft confirms your eligibility.
Not every group qualifies. Google's program excludes government bodies, hospitals and schools, for example. Design tools such as Canva also run nonprofit programs; check their official nonprofit page for current terms. Prices and rules change, so always check the official page before you apply.
Step by step:
- Have your organization's legal name, address and tax-exempt proof ready.
- Open the official Google for Nonprofits and Microsoft nonprofit pages.
- Read the eligibility rules.
- Apply with an organization email, not a personal one.
- Activate each product separately after you are approved.
Words to know:
- Eligible: allowed to join because you meet the rules.
- Tax-exempt: recognized by the government as not paying certain taxes, such as a 501(c)(3) in the United States.
- Ad Grants: Google's program giving qualifying nonprofits free search ads.
Official sources:
- Google for Nonprofits
- Google Ad Grants
- Microsoft offers for nonprofits
Try it now: Open the Google for Nonprofits and Microsoft nonprofit offers pages. Write down whether your organization looks eligible for each and what proof you would need.
You can now find nonprofit tech programs, check eligibility, and know what to have ready to apply.

check.q: What does Microsoft do after you register for its nonprofit offers?
options: Gives you a grant in cash
check.why: You register and Microsoft confirms your eligibility.

check.q: A public school asks you if it can join Google for Nonprofits. What do you tell them?
options: Yes, if they pay a fee
Google's page says schools are excluded, so check the official page
check.why: Google's program excludes government bodies, hospitals and schools.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Setting safe habits for every tool
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Set up an AI tool safely for your team's use.
This lesson builds toward: When your team starts using a tool, you will set it up with an organization account, two-step sign-in and its privacy controls checked, with no private information going in unless leaders approved it.
Use organization accounts, not personal ones, so work stays with the organization when a volunteer moves on. Turn on two-step sign-in for every account.
Learn where each tool keeps your chat history and whether it can be turned off or deleted. Look in the tool's settings for privacy or data controls.
The golden rule is the same in every tool: no donor, volunteer or client private information goes in unless your leaders have approved that tool for it. Use placeholders like [name] instead.
Step by step:
- Sign in with an organization account.
- Turn on two-step sign-in.
- Open settings and find the privacy or data controls.
- Agree as a team: no private information, use placeholders.
Words to know:
- Two-step sign-in: a second check, like a code on your phone, when you log in.
- Chat history: the record a tool keeps of your past conversations.
Try it now: Open the settings of the AI tool you use most. Find where it keeps your chat history and any privacy controls. Write one sentence on what you found.
You can now set up an AI tool with safe habits for your team.

check.q: Where do you find a tool's chat history and data controls?
check.why: Look in the tool's settings for privacy or data controls.

check.q: A volunteer set up the team's design tool on her personal account and is moving away. What should you have done?
options: Used an organization account so the work stays with the organization
check.why: Organization accounts keep work with the organization when a volunteer moves on.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Doing real work with AI tools

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Turning meeting notes into a clear summary
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use a chat assistant to turn rough meeting notes into a summary with action items.
This lesson builds toward: Given rough meeting notes, you will remove private details and use a chat assistant to write a summary with an action-item table, with every decision and date checked against your notes.
Board, ministry team and volunteer meetings produce messy notes. A chat assistant can turn them into a clean summary in seconds.
First remove private details: no names of clients, health issues or donor amounts. Use roles instead: "the treasurer", "the youth lead". Then paste the notes with this prompt: "Summarize these meeting notes in 5 bullet points. Then list action items as a table with: task, who (by role), and due date."
Check the summary against your notes. AI can miss a decision or invent a due date. Fix it, then add real names yourself before you share it.
Step by step:
- Remove private details; use roles instead of names.
- Paste the notes into the chat assistant.
- Ask for a 5-bullet summary and an action-item table.
- Check every decision and date against your notes.
- Add real names yourself, then share.
Words to know:
- Action item: a task someone agreed to do after a meeting.
- Summary: a short version that keeps the main points.
Try it now: Take notes from a recent meeting (or write five lines of practice notes). Remove private details, ask for a summary and an action-item table, and check it against the notes.
You can now turn meeting notes into a checked summary with action items using AI.

check.q: In the summary prompt, how is "who" listed in the action-item table?
check.why: The prompt asks for task, who (by role) and due date; you add names later.

check.q: The AI summary leaves out a decision the board made. What do you do?
options: Ask AI to guess what was decided
Add the decision from your notes before sharing
check.why: Check the summary against your notes and fix anything missed.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Making a volunteer flyer with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI to write flyer text and a design tool to lay it out.
This lesson builds toward: Given a volunteer event, you will create a recruitment flyer with AI-written text and a design tool template, with date, time, place and contact checked and only permitted photos.
Start with the words. Ask a chat assistant: "Write flyer text to recruit volunteers for our Saturday tutoring program for middle schoolers. Include a short headline, three reasons to join, the time commitment, and how to sign up. Under 60 words."
Then open a design tool, search its templates for "volunteer" or "flyer", and paste in your text. Many design tools have AI features that suggest layouts or images; describe what you want and pick one.
Check the details yourself: date, time, place, contact and sign-up link. Use photos you have permission to use, and never show children's faces without written permission from a parent or guardian.
Step by step:
- Ask a chat assistant for short flyer text.
- Open a design tool and search for a flyer template.
- Paste your text and adjust the layout.
- Check date, time, place and contact.
- Use only images you have permission to use.
Words to know:
- Template: a ready-made design you fill in with your own words.
- Permission: agreement, often written, to use someone's photo or work.
Try it now: Make a volunteer recruitment flyer for a real or practice program: AI-written text under 60 words, laid out in a design tool template. Check every detail.
You can now make a volunteer flyer using AI for the words and a design tool for the layout.

check.q: What do you search for in a design tool's templates?
check.why: Search the templates for "volunteer" or "flyer" and paste in your text.

check.q: The AI flyer text lists the wrong sign-up link. What do you do?
options: Fix the link yourself before printing
Ask the design tool to guess the link
check.why: Check date, time, place, contact and sign-up link yourself.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Building your team's AI toolkit card
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a one-page toolkit card that tells your team which tools to use and how.
This lesson builds toward: For your team, you will write a one-page toolkit card that names each approved tool, what it is for and what must never go into it, with your best prompts added and a review date set.
A toolkit card is one page your team can keep beside the computer. It names each approved tool, what it is for, how to sign in, and what must never go into it.
Keep it short: one row per tool. Add the two or three prompts that worked best for your team, like the meeting summary prompt, so new volunteers can copy them.
Review the card every six months. Tools, prices and nonprofit programs change, and your team will discover better prompts.
Step by step:
- List one chat assistant, one office suite and one design tool.
- For each: what it is for and how to sign in.
- Add the privacy rule for each.
- Add your two or three best prompts.
- Set a date to review it in six months.
Words to know:
- Toolkit card: a one-page guide to the tools your team uses and how to use them safely.
Try it now: Final task: write your team's one-page AI toolkit card with three tools, their uses and privacy rules, and attach the meeting summary and flyer you made.
You can now choose, use and document a small set of AI tools for your nonprofit team.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Right tools named Missing one of the three tool kinds, or a tool is used for the wrong job. Names one chat assistant, one office suite and one design tool, each with what it is for. Notes which tools come free or discounted through a nonprofit program. Safety rules on the card The card does not say what must never go into each tool. Each tool says what must never go into it, with organization accounts and two-step sign-in. Also says where to find each tool's privacy controls. Meeting summary The summary has names or private details, or a wrong decision or date. Summary and action-item table by role, checked against the notes. Real names were added only after copying out of the AI tool. Volunteer flyer Wrong or missing date, time, place or contact, or an unpermitted photo. Headline, reasons to join, time commitment and sign-up, all details checked. Uses only photos with permission and is easy to read at a glance. Usable toolkit card More than one page, or missing how to sign in. One page, one row per tool, with the best prompts. Has a review date about six months away and an owner. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: How is a toolkit card laid out?
options: One row per tool on one page
check.why: Keep it short: one page, one row per tool.

check.q: Your team found a meeting prompt that works really well. What do you do with it?
options: Add it to the toolkit card so new volunteers can copy it
check.why: Add the best prompts so new volunteers can copy what works.
